tier_reason: The README's 'Performance Benefits' BenchmarkDotNet table compares SIMD Sum against a Naive loop over int[] with runtime, OS and CPU (i7-10510U) stated, but the benchmark source is not in the repo: SimpleSIMD.sln holds only the SimpleSIMD, Generator and Tests projects, and Tests.csproj references xunit, not BenchmarkDotNet. First-party numbers without public benchmark code are tier C.

corrections.caveats: The benchmark source is not public: SimpleSIMD.sln contains only SimpleSIMD, Generator and Tests, and Tests.csproj is an xunit unit-test project with no BenchmarkDotNet reference, so only the README table can be checked. Only Sum over int[] is benchmarked, against a hand-written scalar loop rather than LINQ Enumerable.Sum. The gain (about 6.7x at 10,000 elements) comes from 8-lane AVX2 Vector<int> against a loop that .NET 7 RyuJIT does not auto-vectorize. The second README table (ValueDelegate vs Delegate) compares the library against itself, with both paths SIMD-accelerated, not against an incumbent. Integer Sum wraps on overflow in both paths. The LinqFaster README states that as of .NET 9 most such optimizations are in the native LINQ library, so the advantage over current runtimes is unmeasured. Last commit 2022-11-19.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly (10: 3.556 vs 5.357 ns; 1000: 66.018 vs 388.244 ns; 10000: 585.275 vs 3,938.198 ns; 100000: 7,325.734 vs 40,283.073 ns). The Sum implementation in SimpleSIMD/Reduction/Sum.cs is a correct vector accumulation plus scalar tail. The entry is C#, not C++ and not callable from C++: shortcomings are no public benchmark code, a naive-loop baseline only, and abandonment (MIT, 93 stars, 174 commits).

tier_reason: The benchmark code is public (internal/functions/*_test.go: BenchmarkSumProd, BenchmarkAdd, BenchmarkLogic and others, each running the *_Go and *_AVX2 variants), and the README gives the go test command, but neither the CPU model nor the Go version is stated, so the evidence falls short of A. These are first-party numbers, so tier C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: go test -benchmem -timeout 0 -run=^# -bench=. ./internal/... ; Go version not stated; the AVX2 kernels are assembly generated from C++ (asm/_cpp with Agner Fog's vectorclass/version2 submodule) compiled with -ffast-math according to the README Notes
corrections.caveats: CPU model, Go version and run count are not stated. The speedup column uses the 100k-element sizes; at 1k some gaps are smaller (vek.Add 484 vs 192 ns, vek.Maximum 1,000 vs 517 ns, vek.And 1,172 vs 60 ns, derived from page data). The 139x vek.And row compares against And_Go, a short-circuit loop 'x[i] = x[i] && y[i]' over random 50% booleans: a branchy worst case for a scalar baseline that a branchless Go loop would narrow. BenchmarkLogic clones the input under StopTimer on every iteration. The Go fallback Sum is a single-accumulator serial loop, and the SIMD kernels are built with -ffast-math, which allows reassociation, so results can differ slightly in precision and are undefined for NaN or Inf inputs (README Notes). The MatMul baseline is the library's own pure-Go loop, not gonum or a BLAS. Acceleration needs x86-64 AVX2 and FMA (no ARM path) and is off by default on macOS. An Any() bug (wrong result for len > 256 and len % 32 > 0, stale RAX in the generated assembly) was fixed in August 2025 (commit 0ce8425). It does not touch any benchmarked row. Last commit (2025-09-06) is a README note on fast math.

notes: All claimed numbers appear in the README table (vek32.Sum 65,007 vs 3,191 ns 20x; vek32.Exp 22x; vek32.Log 16x; vek32.Add 6x; vek.Add 2x; MatMul 7x and 14x; vek.And 139x; Quantile 1x). The baseline is the library's own pure-Go fallback (plain Go loops), a reasonable stand-in for idiomatic Go. Shortcomings: Go, not C++; no CPU or Go version; fast-math semantics; the 139x And row is inflated by a branchy short-circuit baseline. Metadata checked: MIT, 204 stars, 19 commits, not a fork, last commit 2025-09-06 (stale).
